# Overview {.unnumbered}

**MOOOD-study** is a *discrete-event simulation* (built on **SimPy**) of people who ring
NHS 111, the non-emergency health advice line. At the end of the call the call handler
gives the caller an outcome, called a *disposition*, such as Dx05, which the code
labels "contact" with a 2-hour time frame. The model simulates many such callers and follows each for 72 hours
as they go on to contact a GP, 111 again, 999 (the emergency number), the emergency
department (ED) or inpatient care (admission to hospital). It samples these onward contacts
from **empirical transition probabilities** and **fitted time distributions** loaded from
the `csv/` folder. Several independent replications run in parallel with `multiprocessing`,
and each writes an **event log** and **network edge counts** to CSV. The simulated pattern
is then compared with real data from *Connected Yorkshire*, a regional database that links patients'
health records.

You use it through a web app built with **Plotly Dash**. You configure a run (duration,
warm-up, number of runs, a *what-if* scenario in which every caller gets timely GP contact,
and alternative transition and arrival methods), press **Run Simulation**, and then view
the results as charts, Sankey diagrams (flow diagrams), tables and a Cytoscape network graph.

The code accompanies a published feasibility study, Pilbery et al. (2023) in *BMJ Open*, and a talk given for HSMA (Health Service Modelling Associates, an NHS training scheme in simulation and data science). For the research question, the data and how the code differs from the paper, read [The study behind the model](background.qmd) first.

## Running the code

Locally, run `python index.py`. Alternatively, follow the repository README to build and
start the Docker container, then open <http://localhost:8080/>.

## Where to start

- New to NHS urgent care? Start with [The study behind the model](background.qmd).
- New to simulation? Read chapters 1 to 3 in order.
- Only interested in the model? Start at chapter 3.
- Only interested in the charts? Jump to chapter 8.

## Terms you will meet

111 is the NHS non-emergency advice line and 999 the emergency number. ED is the emergency
department, IP is inpatient care, and GP is the general practitioner. IUC is integrated
urgent care (the service behind 111), so `Index_IUC` is the first 111 call. A disposition is
the outcome code given at the end of the 111 call, and HSM is the Health Service Model
class. See the [Glossary](glossary.qmd) for more.

**Source repository:** <https://github.com/ReModel-Club/MOOOD-study>

## Chapters

1. [Dash Application Shell](01_dash_application_shell.qmd) — How the Dash app starts, routes between pages and stores run settings in the browser.
2. [Run Configuration and Orchestration](02_run_configuration_and_orchestration.qmd) — How form values become global parameters and launch parallel simulation runs.
3. [Health Service Model](03_health_service_model.qmd) — How one HSM replication sets up the SimPy environment and generates 111 calls over time.
4. [Caller and Call Dispositions](04_caller_and_call_dispositions.qmd) — What a simulated caller is and how its disposition and GP contact are sampled.
5. [Patient Journey Process](05_patient_journey_process.qmd) — How each caller is moved from service to service for 72 hours as a SimPy process.
6. [Transitions and Time Distributions](06_transitions_and_time_distributions.qmd) — How next destinations, wait times, visit durations and avoidable ED attendances are sampled.
7. [Simulation Event Log and Network Data](07_simulation_event_log_and_network_data.qmd) — What the model records for each event and transition and how it is written to CSV.
8. [Results Dashboard and Visualisation](08_results_dashboard_and_visualisation.qmd) — How results callbacks turn simulation CSVs and observed data into charts, tables and graphs.

Terms introduced along the way are collected in the [Glossary](glossary.qmd).
